lines.label: Bill Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. It's hard to believe it's halfway— April is halfway gone and there's only 2 weeks left to file personal income tax. Tax filing is an important event required by Canada Revenue Service. Before April 30th. And if by chance you have a refund coming, you want to get it done as soon as possible. This leads me to an article on Steinbach Online done by Shannon Dewick, used by permission. Steinbach most generous city in Canada. According to recent data from Statistics Canada, southern Manitoba trends well above average when it comes to charitable giving. In Canada as a whole, The average tax filer donates $380 towards charity. And in Manitoba, this number is considerably higher. It's $590. But when you consider southeastern Manitoba, the top 4 communities are as follows: Blumenort, an average of $3,780; Kleefeld at $2,320; and Steinbach at $2,240. Followed by Grunthal at $1,990. Steinbach being the most generous city in all of Canada with a population of 10,000 or higher. According to one article, Steinbach residents donated 4.31% of their income to charity, and that is a full percent higher than the city next to them. Giving is a key component to the success of our community. People in Steinbach are very generous in giving time, with volunteering, plus giving their money to many of our charities. I'm reminded of key projects that would not have happened if it wasn't for local fundraising, both by businesses and private. Our Rest Haven Nursing Home is serving our seniors in a tremendous way. That wouldn't have happened with fundraising. The much anticipated event center, which is in progress, and also the Bethesda Hospital expansion with the new surgery theaters, kidney dialysis, and other facilities as well. Some real benefits for being generous, top 5 according to survey done by Harvard Business School. Giving makes us feel happy. Giving has been linked to the release of oxytocin, a hormone that includes feelings of warmth, euphoria, and connection to others. Number 2, giving is good for our health. Research shows that seniors who volunteered at 2 or more organizations were 44% less likely to die over a 5-year period. Number 3 is giving promotes cooperation and social connection. When we give to others, we don't only make them feel closer to us, we also feel closer to them. Being kind and generous leads you to perceive others Positively. Number 4 is giving evokes gratitude. Whether you're on the giving or receiving end of a gift, that gift can elicit feelings of gratitude. Number 5 is giving is contagious. When giving, we don't only help the recipient with their gift, but also spur on a ripple effect of giving in our community. So let's continue giving cheerfully. Thank you. Thank you.

lines.text: Thank you. The— getting to the task at hand, the traffic count report, as you mentioned, that has recently been completed for the corner of Loewen Boulevard and Hespeler Street in Steinbach was undertaken by administration, as you mentioned, at the request of council. And in addition to the annual fall traffic count and analysis that the city normally undertakes, a specific additional component was undertaken at this intersection. The traffic counts at this corner were done for several years beginning beginning in 2019. Given that there hadn't been significant change over a three-year period, those counts were were suspended. However, there appear to be periodic concerns expressed to members of council from residents of Steinbach, which prompted council's request for administration to review this corner again. With respect to that review, generally traffic flows and the level of service at their The traffic counts at this intersection are very well understood. As I mentioned, City of Steinbach retained WSP Canada Group Limited to provide the traffic analysis. And generally, the results from that count did show that there is a fairly even distribution of traffic between the 3 legs that meet at that intersection. I won't read the entirety of the report. There are details in there both from the city's engineer and also from WSP, the city's consultants, but I would direct council to the general summary and final conclusions towards the bottom of page 3 of the report from the city's engineer. And based on WSP's assessment of the intersections or of the intersection, no improvements are considered Yes. The results of the analysis were not considered required given the northbound Hespeler's level of service of E, which from a standard analysis that the city uses when it evaluates intersections across Steinbach is acceptable. However, it goes on to say the results did show that it would improve the overall level of service for the intersection during the PM peak hour scenario at the cost of longer delays for the Loewen Boulevard westbound and eastbound traffic Okay. If changes were made, and this, however, would also expect that at all other times of the day, since that traffic along Loewen Boulevard would no longer be free-flowing, ultimately, the level of service for that through traffic as it exists today would be negatively affected. Generally, from the city's engineer, in conclusion, The city should collect more data to fully understand the cause and of the delays before making a change to this intersection since an all-way stop controlled intersection could result in some unintended consequences for the Loewen Boulevard traffic. And given the inconclusiveness of the analysis and that this intersection will need to become an all-way stop controlled Yes. So, the idea of moving the intersection at the time that the city initiates the PTH 12 and Loewen Boulevard project, which is a mile further to the west, that's something that administration is considering just because of the degree of traffic disruption that is expected from that ultimate detour that would be required during that project. So in other words, what is being recommended is that while no permanent change to that intersection is being recommended at this time, especially pursuant to further consideration of a traffic roundabout that may be designed in the future, there is perhaps an opportunity to consider an all-way stop. Okay. in the event that the city does proceed with the PTH 12 and Loewen Boulevard intersection improvements at some point in the future.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I made this request, uh, for a 3-way stop at this intersection. I think I did it twice in my term on council. I think, uh, The information that was collected by WSP, and it also says it in the engineer's report, that more data is needed to be collected. And I'm not a traffic engineer by any stretch, but I also use that intersection, and I get a lot of different comments on it from people that do read that, use that intersection. I appreciate the report. It's very comprehensive. It provides us with a lot of details, but not all the details. The conclusion in both cases is that there's more data needs to be collected before final decision, and both reports indicate a traffic circle would solve the issue as well. And I certainly agree with that because a traffic circle would solve those issues at that intersection. Both reports mention the one thing— hesitant drivers, the one thing we can't control at council. And one, the drivers wanting to make a left-hand turn that's hesitant off of Hespeler onto Loewen Boulevard. In my opinion, it is a top reason we need to move forward with the 3-corner stop. Pedestrian traffic is mentioned in the report, but it is not told us how it is affected by this intersection. For the last 20-plus years, council has promoted active transportation in some form. We put up maps indicating different Walking and bike paths. We paint signs on our roadways to remind us, both cyclists and motorists, where to travel and install our share the road signs. This intersection is part of an active transportation route. A bike lane has been identified by paintings on the road, both on Hespeler and Loewen, both going— each going each way. A cyclist going north on Hespeler, like I was doing last Friday afternoon at quarter to 3, And I forgot to turn earlier. I wanted to avoid that intersection, but I got there. I wanted to make a left-hand turn onto Loewen. That's a very exciting and scary time during many parts of the day. But the cyclist needs to be aware of traffic going from east to west, also right-hand turning traffic that's going from Hespeler onto Loewen Boulevard. Loewen Boulevard is a correction mile road. Hence the offset. Traveling anywhere in Loewen in any direction, the intersections are offset. In the late 1980s, Steinbach Council put up a 3-corner stop at Henry and Loewen. The reasons were to slow down speeding traffic, but more so to allow the pedestrians to cross safely when the new pathway was built going north. There are many moving pieces to this corner. No stop flow By not stopping east-west flow traffic on Loewen Boulevard. It's a major pedestrian crossing, bicycle crossing, and turning movements. Hesitant drivers and motorists not indicating what action they are taking by not using their turn signals in a timely manner. Another thing that we can't— we can only complain about it. The report indicates that this intersection will be a full stop, full all-way stop for 2 years during construction of Loewen and number 12. That makes sense. We've talked about that. Hopefully that project will start later this year. It is my opinion that we should move forward with making this a 3-way stop for all the reasons mentioned above. While it will slow down traffic going east and west on Loewen, it will make it safer for pedestrians and cyclists and move traffic more effectively during peak times. Since it will be changing a 3-way stop from— when construction starts on Loewen and 12th, we can move that timeline forward a few months and have those stop signs in in place. But the most exciting thing is that both reports said that a roundabout would fix this intersection.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Anything further?

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Further to what Councillor Siemens said, and yes, I do agree with what has just been presented, if we go to page 3 on the report, second last paragraph, it talks about the intersection that Brandt, or number 12, and Loewen, when that construction starts. And it says this detour would be required for a minimum of 2-year period. If the intersection were to ultimately change to an all-stop control, the change could be made at this time after further analysis and would be seen as less controversial. I don't agree with that we need further study, further analysis. I think there's been enough complaints and I think enough observations made of this intersection that it would definitely benefit. I don't think it's a controversial issue that we're trying to avoid. I think it's a necessity to put in all the stop signs at all 3, the 3-way stop. I think that's necessary and I too have advocated for it in the past and I continue to advocate for it. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Councillor Zwaagstra.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. This is a very interesting discussion. I'm not sure why we bothered to get this traffic analysis because it sounds like members of council have got their own analysis ready to go. I have some concerns with the motion. I'm going to be voting against it. The reason that we hire experts to do this kind of analysis using standards and in evaluating the overall situation is so that we don't end up with the law of unintended consequences. We don't want to have a situation where we're just adding stop signs because we feel that that is the best approach to go. So what's been identified here is that there's obviously some challenges with this intersection. And when the Loewen Boulevard and Highway 12 construction begins, at that point, as it says here, at that point, because there will be all this additional traffic, we will have to, for that time period, make it an all-way stop. Okay. Which makes sense. So then let's do it at that time because that is when the experts that we've hired, that's our staff and also our consultants who have actually analyzed this intersection, have said is the best time to do it. It's important to note here that our report says, identifies that an all-way stop-controlled intersection could result in unintended consequences for Loewen Boulevard traffic. So we see a problem and we immediately think that we've got a solution. Right. So we need to be careful here because there's a longer-term picture that we need to pay— we need to take. And I don't see why we got this report, why we had this analysis done going through, you know, the different— some of the different options here, pointing out that there needs to be a longer-term picture here, and then we've got a motion that, yeah, no, never mind what's in here, we're just going to go ahead and do it because we've already got our analysis and we've just identified that needs to be solved. We don't know We want that Loewen Boulevard intersection to go ahead this year. We're still waiting on certain things to be confirmed. So we don't want to just rush ahead with changing the stop signs here prior to that going ahead. So let's, let's actually trust our staff and our experts and the analysis that we have. And let's not just go start making up our own, our own decisions all of a sudden that we're going to just decide we know better here. So we need to, we need to proceed carefully. So I'm going to vote against the motion. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Go ahead, Councillor.

lines.speaker: Bill Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Bill Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you. I personally— oh, I'm voting for it because I've had the experience of sitting at that corner with Hesston drivers ahead of myself. I timed out 5 minutes last summer with a Hesston driver sitting at the stop sign and didn't make a left turn. And it's the left turn that's the main issue, and it's very frustrating. There were probably 15 cars behind me, so So it is— I think it's a fairly serious issue. And also traffic speeds up at that point and it would slow down traffic as well. So I think that would be beneficial as well.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Go ahead, Councillor.

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I also will not be supporting the motion. There was no place in the report from the experts that we commissioned to do this that that was the recommendation going forward. The recommendation was to Get more information. And prime way of getting that information is going to be with how the construction is going to be affected with— or how the construction is going to be affecting there, and then us putting in an all-way stop. And that's a great time for us to be able to get the information of what we do need to do with that intersection going forward. I'm not going to deny that there is challenges with that intersection, but we are not the traffic experts and we don't know what challenges are going to be increased or new challenges going to be coming up by doing an all-way stop there. So I have a saying, and that is let the plumbers plumb, and I'm going to let the experts and the traffic experts tell us what to do on this one.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, thank you. Councillor Penner.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: I'll be voting against the motion as well. There's a saying that says hard cases make bad laws, and I think to a certain degree that applies here. We're hearing from, you know, one-off personal situations. One time, Councillor Hiebert had to sit for 5 minutes and maybe one time somebody— this experience happened to Councillor Siemens or the other councillor, Hiebert. The point of the study is that we get a broad picture of what's going on. We can't base it on our one-off personal experiences because then we're going to make very poor decisions. Not this with— just with this, but with other things. The reality is there's rush hour times in every community and city. We see rush hour. On the number 12 highway. And we see rush hour on this street when school lets out. That's the reality of living in a big community in a big city. So I don't think we should change, particularly based on what the report says, we should now go and make these changes based on, you know, there's a peak time where it takes 5 minutes to get through there when the other, you know, 23+ hours of the day or whatever it is, it's— I think that's a good point. Not really that significant of an issue. I would have serious concerns how this would affect Loewen Boulevard east-west traffic. Does that make sense? Yes. And so I, again, I would think that would certainly slow down traffic and have a negative impact there. You know, this is on the radar. We're going to see how it works when we're doing— when we have to have the 3-way stop there. So I don't know why we would jump the gun on this at this point when, yeah, when we don't need to. So I will not be supporting the motion.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything in closing?

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Yes. The, the words unintended consequences, I use that often myself when, when we make decisions. I've used it often at council trying to understand. We don't know what the unintended consequences are here. I do know that there's a problem. At that place for pedestrians to cross, for cyclists to, to be part of that corner. I do know there's lots of hesitant drivers. Yes, I'm not an engineer, traffic engineer. I don't. But I know how people behave at that corner, and that— I know that corner doesn't function properly many times during the day. So for all those reasons, as mentioned here, I think it is important for me to state the case here. Thank you. And I was the one who has been promoting a roundabout in the first place, and we had that opportunity 2 years ago when we had the corner ripped apart. I also now think the second best option is to put a 3-corner stop, and the third option is to do nothing. And to do nothing, I think, would fail that corner.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Council, I enjoy hearing the discussion back and forth. I really like this. I too will vote against the motion. I too have apprehensions in changing the corner for 24 hours when it's just a half-hour to 45-minute problem. I use that corner a lot. I never ever go, like, I don't avoid that corner and I haven't experienced I've experienced delays, maybe 3 minutes, but I've never experienced the delays you guys have experienced. And I have been 10th, 15th car on Hespeler. Maybe my day I'm there just works out better, but I think that if we go and we go change this before we have more information or before We're ready with the— for it to be the detour. I think we circumvent what we've done here, and I think the best plan is probably to keep working and get the roundabout in our long-term capital plan and get that project done. And then that intersection will be fixed forever, and it'll all— traffic will always flow. Thank you. Always flow, 'cause roundabouts are really the best thing for traffic flow. Call for the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is defeated. Can you— Yep. I have to excuse myself for just a minute.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, council, we will head to administration 9C, business licenses. That is on page 109. And, uh, can I get a motion to approve the business license? Councillor Susan Penner, seconded by Councillor Damian Penner. Any discussion?

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: No discussion.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Anything for Councillor Penner?

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: No, sir.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, I'll call the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. We head to 9D, Bylaw 2243, Tax Certificate Fee Bylaw, first reading. Mr. Warkentin, can you introduce this one, please?

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Deputy Mayor. This bylaw, number 2243, is a bylaw to update the city's tax certificate fee amounts that are charged to the public. The current tax certificate fee Yes. Tax certificate fee bylaw number 1820 has been in place since 2007, which is 17 years. And because tax certificate fees are set by bylaw, the city generally does not amend that bylaw fairly often. However, it was actually surprising to realize how long it has actually been in place. And because that is noted within the Municipal Act This particular fee is set by bylaw. Recommendation from administration is that council give this bylaw first reading so that the current tax fee certificate or tax certificate fee amount can be updated.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Council, could I get a motion, please? Councillor Siemens, seconded by— sorry, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Motion to approve.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Seconded by Councillor Susan Penner. Councillor Siemens, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: As explained by administration, this is a fee charged for tax certificates. I don't know all the details around it, but I believe administration has guided us.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, thank you. Councillor Penner, do you wish to add anything?

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: I don't know what I can add. Is that a clear explanation? I don't know what I can possibly add to that. This is first reading, so we'll be seeing this again.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Okay. Anything further from council? Anything in closing, Councillor Siemens?

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: I think that was quite enough.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Well, council, I will, I will vote in favour as well. I mean, our city staff has— our city manager has made it clear that this is a matter of updating a previous bylaw, and, you know, fees do rise over time, and part of the goal here is to ensure that we are recovering our costs and that our rates are comparable with neighbouring municipalities. So I don't have any problem with this change either. So I'll call the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. We go to 9E, Bylaw 2247. That's the 2024 Realty and Education Tax Levy Bylaw, our budget. Uh, Mr. Warkentin, you want to introduce this one too?

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Uh, yes, Mr. Deputy Mayor. Bylaw 2247 is the bylaw to authorize the city's 2024 Realty and Education Tax Regarding Levy. the 2024 education taxes for the City of Steinbach, the city's mill rate will be set at a total of 14.4 mills for 2023— or sorry, for 2024. Recommendation is that council give Bylaw 2247 first reading.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Okay. Council, how would you like to proceed? Councillor Hiebert, seconded by Councillor Bill Hiebert. So Councillor Hewitt, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Deputy Mayor. What we have here is an application by administration. They've done their work and it's come to us that the 2024 realty and education tax levy has been set per mill rate and the mill rate is 14.4 mills. That is what we require to pay this administration fee. This fee for the Hanover School Division levy, which is increased, and the mill rate was set for them for 7.54, while the provincial levy has increased 4.8 mill rates. So it's obviously what we require to make ends meet. So this is first reading, and so I approve of it. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, Councillor Hiebert.

lines.speaker: Bill Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Bill Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Deputy Mayor. I, I believe taxes need to be collected, so this is a good move.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, anything further from council? Anything in closing?

lines.label: Unidentified (possibly Jake Hiebert) [low]
lines.text: Nothing further.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, well, council, this is our budget. Uh, as we do every year, uh, we first pass it in principle at, uh, at the, uh, first meeting in April, and then our staff formalizes it into a bylaw. And this, of course, is the bylaw here with the, with with all the numbers in, including the information from the school division. And so since we all unanimously approved the budget that we set, it certainly would make sense for us to also approve the bylaw that comes out from that budget. So I will obviously be voting in favor. I'll call the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. We now go to 9F, Bylaw 2248, the Business Tax Levy Bylaw. Alderman Warkentin, can you introduce this one, please?

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Deputy Mayor. This particular bylaw, number 224— sorry, 8, is the annual business tax levy bylaw to authorize the city to levy and collect business taxes for business property within the city of Steinbach. The proposed tax levy rate for 2024 is 0.5%, and this rate remains unchanged from the previous year. Recommendation for council to give this bylaw first reading.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, thank you. Council, how would you like to proceed? Councillor Susan Penner.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Motion to approve.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Motion to approve, seconded by Councillor Bill Hiebert. Councillor Penner, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Yeah, this tax is basically an in and out for the city. We collect the tax and then we turn it over to the Chamber of Commerce. I think what's interesting and important to note is because it's based on a percentage, the amount they're collecting increases as the city grows and as our assessment goes up. So, and it's also important to note that the business community seemingly supports this tax and this arrangement that this money goes to fund the Chamber of Commerce. So for that, those reasons, or for that reason, I will I'll make the motion here.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Councillor Hiebert.

lines.speaker: Bill Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Bill Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: No further comment.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Okay. Anything further from council? Anything in closing?

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Nothing further.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Well, council, the business tax rate has remained set at 0.5% for many years now, and this is a longstanding arrangement that the city remits this amount minus a small administration fee to the Chamber of Commerce for their operating funds. And so this is an This is something that's been in place for quite some time. So I will vote in favour of first reading as well. So I'll call the question. All those in favour? Opposed? That is carried.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you very much, Deputy Mayor. Okay, number 10, uh, council, uh, council question period. Any council, uh, questions of council? Okay, seeing none, we've got one item of correspondence. This is the, um, Minister of Municipality and Northern Relations and Minister of Indigenous and Economic Development. This is, uh, the summary of the budget, the 2024 budget. Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I have a report for the available funding to municipalities, and we've all had a chance to review. Council, how would you like to proceed? Take his information at this time? There's no other business. Looking for a motion to adjourn. Second. Second by Councillor Siemens. Call for the question. All those in favor? That is carried. Next council, regular council meeting is Tuesday, May 7th, 2024.
